name: Cruise
founding_story: Kyle Vogt started Cruise in 2013 to commercialize autonomous driving, initially through an aftermarket highway-driving system for existing cars. [Source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruise_%28autonomous_vehicle%29)
founders_background: Kyle Vogt: technical entrepreneur who previously co-founded Justin.tv, Twitch and Socialcam. Daniel Kan: previously worked at UserVoice and founded Exec. [Vogt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle_Vogt) [Kan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Kan_%28executive%29)

pre_funding_traces.note: No public product launch or customer traction verified before YC W14; the public RP-1 announcement came afterward.

how_they_got_funded: Cruise attended YC W14 and raised $4.3 million in convertible debt following Demo Day; a $13 million Series A led by Spark Capital followed in 2015. [Demo Day](https://fortune.com/longform/cruise-automation-general-motors-driverless-cars/) [Series A](https://multiples.vc/private-comps/cruise)
first_round_after_yc: $4.3 million convertible-debt seed financing, 2014. [Source](https://fortune.com/longform/cruise-automation-general-motors-driverless-cars/)
pivots: Shifted from aftermarket highway-driving kits to fully autonomous vehicles in 2015; GM subsequently redirected the technology toward personal vehicles. [History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruise_%28autonomous_vehicle%29) [GM](https://investor.gm.com/news-releases/news-release-details/gm-refocus-autonomous-driving-development-personal-vehicles/)
outcome: GM acquired control in 2016, completed the remaining ownership acquisition in February 2025, and began winding down robotaxi operations. [Source](https://www.sec.gov/ixviewer/ix.html?doc=%2FArchives%2Fedgar%2Fdata%2F1467858%2F000146785825000096%2Fgm-20250331.htm)

failure_reasons.explanation: GM ended robotaxi funding because scaling required considerable additional time and resources.
GM explicitly cited the increasingly competitive robotaxi market.
California suspended driverless operating permission after a pedestrian incident; an independent review identified leadership and regulator-relationship failures.

key_lesson: Interpretation: technical progress and acquisition success do not eliminate the need for safe operations, regulatory trust and a scalable business model.

name: Machine Zone
founding_story: Gabriel Leydon, Halbert Nakagawa and Mike Sherrill founded Addmired in 2008, initially building MySpace social widgets before moving into mobile games. The original motivation beyond those products is unknown. [Source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Zone)
founders_background: Gabriel Leydon: seven years in arcade games at Atari, Tsunami Visual and Global VR. Mike Sherrill: previously an Atari play tester. Halbert Nakagawa: founding CTO; earlier employment and education unknown. [Leydon](https://www.pocketgamer.biz/industry/gabe-leydon/) [Sherrill](https://podcasts.apple.com/no/podcast/founders-story-machine-zone-with-mike-sherrill/id1482684742?i=1000519841278) [Nakagawa](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/machine-zone)

pre_funding_traces.note: No independently dated public trace verified before YC W08 funding; the later mobile games do not qualify.

how_they_got_funded: The company launched with YC funding in 2008. It later raised $5.3 million from Anthos Capital and Baseline Ventures, followed by an $8 million Series B from Menlo Ventures in March 2012; the YC application story and any intervening seed round are unknown. [Source](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/addmired-reveals-new-name-announces-new-funding-social-games-pioneer-shervin-pishevar-joins-board-144353675.html)
first_round_after_yc: unknown
pivots: MySpace social widgets became free-to-play multiplayer mobile games; Addmired renamed itself Machine Zone in 2012. A later expansion into real-time infrastructure was followed by renewed emphasis on gaming. [History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Zone) [Refocus](https://www.fastcompany.com/90263128/how-the-maker-of-mobile-hit-game-of-war-lost-unpivoted-itself)
outcome: AppLovin acquired Machine Zone in May 2020; it subsequently became part of Tripledot Studios through the 2025 acquisition of AppLovin's games business. [2020](https://d18rn0p25nwr6d.cloudfront.net/CIK-0001751008/cc415626-ad35-47ee-9edc-c0d66214e830.pdf) [Current ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Zone)
key_lesson: Interpretation: an unsuccessful social product can become a substantial business when founders find a better application for their product and engineering capabilities.

name: Oklo
founding_story: Jacob DeWitte and Caroline Cochran started the company in 2013 to commercialize smaller advanced nuclear reactors through incremental development requiring less capital than conventional nuclear projects. It was originally incorporated as UPower Technologies. [MIT](https://news.mit.edu/2020/oklo-nuclear-energy-1113) [Filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000110465924073383/R118.htm)
founders_background: Jacob DeWitte: MIT nuclear-engineering PhD student when developing the venture. Caroline Cochran: MIT master's in nuclear engineering, with undergraduate degrees in economics and mechanical engineering from the University of Oklahoma. [DeWitte](https://news.mit.edu/2013/clean-energy-prize-awards-0507) [Cochran](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/oklo)

pre_funding_traces.note: UPower won the infrastructure/resources category of the MIT Clean Energy Prize in May 2013, before its July incorporation; the ordering relative to its first 2013 investment is unknown, so this is an early public trace rather than a confirmed pre-investment trace.
Strictly pre-investment chronology could not be established: MIT reports small funding rounds in 2013 and 2014 without precise dates.

how_they_got_funded: Small rounds in 2013 and 2014 accompanied MassChallenge and YC participation. Sam Altman met the founders in 2013 and recruited them into YC S14, citing deep technical expertise and leadership; subsequent private investment rounds occurred in 2015 and 2018. [MIT](https://news.mit.edu/2020/oklo-nuclear-energy-1113) [Altman](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000110465923079993/tm2321076-3_425.htm) [Round history](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5b5a380231d4df96186b0298/t/5fd27d00bd9896188f836161/1607630086343/Oklo-Intro-AK-Alliance-1220.pdf)
first_round_after_yc: Private investment round in 2015; amount and lead unknown. [Source](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5b5a380231d4df96186b0298/t/5fd27d00bd9896188f836161/1607630086343/Oklo-Intro-AK-Alliance-1220.pdf)
pivots: The reactor design changed substantially during development; no separate business-model pivot was verified. [Source](https://news.mit.edu/2020/oklo-nuclear-energy-1113)
outcome: Public on the NYSE as OKLO following its May 2024 combination with AltC; it remains an advanced-fission and fuel-recycling developer. [Merger](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000110465924073383/R118.htm) [Company](https://oklo.com/about/company-overview)
key_lesson: Interpretation: deep-technology founders can attract venture funding by combining technical expertise with incremental commercialization milestones.

name: Wave
founding_story: The founders entered YC with Chime, a social app, then launched Sendwave in 2014 after Drew Durbin's experience sending money to Tanzania exposed remittance problems. They began building domestic African mobile money in 2016 to address expensive, inaccessible financial services. [Founder account](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/2023/10/23/entrepreneurship_advice.html) [Company history](https://www.wave.com/jobboard_example.html)
founders_background: Drew Durbin: previously started an NGO in Tanzania and handled distribution, design, partnerships and compliance in the early venture. Co-founder Lincoln Quirk, omitted from the input: Brown computer-science graduate who left a Harvard PhD program and built the software. [Durbin](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/2023/10/23/entrepreneurship_advice.html) [Quirk](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/resume.html)

pre_funding_traces.note: Before YC, predecessor Chime spread across a college campus through an organized group posting daily; usage collapsed when the founders stopped prompting posts. Quirk says this demonstrated execution and distribution to YC.

how_they_got_funded: Chime's demonstrated ability to build and distribute a product helped secure YC admission in 2012. The earliest post-YC financing is unknown; the later Wave mobile-money business raised a $200 million Series A in 2021, jointly led by Sequoia Heritage, Founders Fund, Stripe and Ribbit Capital. [Founder account](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/2023/10/23/entrepreneurship_advice.html) [Series A](https://techcabal.com/2021/10/18/coura-sene-reflects-on-waves-rapid-growth/)
first_round_after_yc: unknown
pivots: Chime social-app experiments became Sendwave remittances in 2014, followed by domestic Wave mobile money development in 2016 and Senegal launch at the end of 2017. [Founder](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/2023/10/23/entrepreneurship_advice.html) [Company](https://www.wave.com/jobboard_example.html)
outcome: Wave remains an operating African mobile-money business. Sendwave was a separate carve-out acquired by WorldRemit in February 2021; that acquisition should not be attributed to Wave Mobile Money. [Wave](https://www.wave.com/jobboard_example.html) [Acquisition filing](https://assets.ctfassets.net/sb7j5o4oxtgv/1px52RScz6YPAHXo6S3UkG/dd0813b08308a97ea50b57a7b6880d6c/WR_Group_Limited_Stat_FY21_ISA_accounts.docx.pdf)
key_lesson: Interpretation: personally experienced financial pain and direct customer investigation can support conviction in a difficult opportunity after easier ideas fail.

name: Segment
founding_story: Segment began in 2011 as a classroom tool for measuring student confusion. After that and an analytics product failed, the founders released their internal analytics-routing library, which became the successful business. [Source](https://segment.com/blog/show-hn-to-series-d/)
founders_background: Ilya Volodarsky: MIT student and product engineer, with prior Microsoft and MIT Media Lab experience. Other co-founders omitted from the input were Peter Reinhardt, an MIT aerospace-engineering student; Calvin French-Owen, an MIT student and backend engineer; and Ian Storm Taylor, a RISD designer/developer. [Ilya](https://www.ycombinator.com/founders/ilya-volodarsky) [MIT founders](https://tollbit.forbes.com/sites/laurencebradford/2017/09/12/success-without-a-diploma-how-3-mit-dropouts-made-it-big/) [Ian](https://wellfound.com/company/segment)

pre_funding_traces.note: No public trace verified before YC S11 funding; the frequently cited analytics.js GitHub and Show HN launch occurred in late 2012, after the 2011 seed round.

how_they_got_funded: Accepted into YC S11 with the classroom product, the founders raised approximately $600,000 at Demo Day before discovering that students did not use it as intended. Later product-market fit came from analytics.js rather than the original funded idea. [YC interview](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/peter-reinhardt-on-finding-product-market-fit-at-segment?endTime=300.00&startTime=288.00) [Company history](https://segment.com/blog/show-hn-to-series-d/)
first_round_after_yc: Seed approximately $600,000, September 2011; lead unknown. [Sources](https://segment.com/blog/show-hn-to-series-d/) [Amount](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/peter-reinhardt-on-finding-product-market-fit-at-segment?endTime=300.00&startTime=288.00)
pivots: Classroom lecture software became a segmentation-focused analytics competitor, then an analytics-routing/customer-data platform after the late-2012 analytics.js release. [Source](https://segment.com/blog/show-hn-to-series-d/)
outcome: Twilio completed its acquisition on November 2, 2020, in a transaction announced at approximately $3.2 billion. [Source](https://investors.twilio.com/node/6966/ixbrl-viewer)
key_lesson: Interpretation: a small internal tool that solves a demonstrated developer problem can be more valuable than the elaborate product originally funded.

name: GOAT Group
founding_story: The YC company began as GrubWithUs, a social-dining service inspired by the founders' difficulty making friends after moving to Chicago. After that business failed, Daishin Sugano's purchase of counterfeit sneakers inspired an authenticated sneaker marketplace. [Source](https://review.firstround.com/goats-path-to-product-market-fit/)
founders_background: Eddy Lu: UC Berkeley computer-science graduate and former Lehman Brothers employee. Daishin Sugano: design background; detailed education and earlier employment unknown. Together they previously operated cream-puff franchises and built iPhone apps. [Lu](https://labusinessjournal.com/special-editions/la500/2022-la500/manufacturing-2022/la500-2022-eddy-lu/) [Joint history](https://review.firstround.com/goats-path-to-product-market-fit/)

pre_funding_traces.note: The founders built paid iPhone apps in 2008, before YC W11; these were earlier founder projects, not GOAT marketplace traction.

how_they_got_funded: GrubWithUs entered YC W11, then raised a $1.6 million seed round including First Round Capital and a $5 million Series A in 2012. Investors subsequently supported the GOAT pivot and allowed the founders to retain the remaining capital. [Source](https://review.firstround.com/goats-path-to-product-market-fit/)
first_round_after_yc: Seed $1.6 million, 2011, including First Round Capital; lead unknown. [Source](https://review.firstround.com/goats-path-to-product-market-fit/)
pivots: GrubWithUs social dining, followed by unsuccessful restaurant-related iterations, became GOAT's authenticated sneaker marketplace, launched in 2015. [Pivot account](https://review.firstround.com/goats-path-to-product-market-fit/) [Launch](https://www.forbes.com/sites/kurtbadenhausen/2019/02/07/foot-locker-invests-100-million-in-secondary-sneaker-firm-goat/)
outcome: Still operating as GOAT Group; the company combined with Flight Club in 2018 and later expanded beyond sneakers. [History](https://www.forbes.com/sites/kurtbadenhausen/2019/02/07/foot-locker-invests-100-million-in-secondary-sneaker-firm-goat/) [Company](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/goat-group)
key_lesson: Interpretation: a pivot works better when it addresses a concrete customer problem than when it merely reuses assets from a failed idea.

name: Scale AI
founding_story: Alexandr Wang and Lucy Guo started Scale in 2016 as an API for outsourced human tasks after seeing how manually intensive content moderation was at Quora and Snapchat. The service developed into infrastructure for AI training data and evaluation. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/scale) [Company](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/scale-ai)
founders_background: Alexandr Wang: MIT student who left to build Scale. Co-founder Lucy Guo, omitted from the input: Carnegie Mellon dropout and Thiel Fellow, with experience at Quora and Snap. [Wang](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hRfgIxNDSgQ) [Guo](https://www.ycombinator.com/founders/lucy-guo) [Education](https://research.contrary.com/company/scale?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)

pre_funding_traces.note: No product trace verified before first outside funding; the documented public launch was during YC S16, and contemporary reporting also mentions Arena VC seed backing without establishing its timing relative to YC.

how_they_got_funded: YC backed the opportunity to improve outsourced human tasks beyond Mechanical Turk. Contemporary coverage also records Arena VC backing; Scale subsequently announced a $4.5 million Accel-led Series A in July 2017. [YC rationale](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/scale) [Early backing](https://techcrunch.com/2016/07/25/scale-lets-companies-outsource-their-human-powered-tasks-with-one-line-of-code/) [Series A](https://scale.com/blog/announcing-our-series-a-with-accel)
first_round_after_yc: Earliest verified named post-YC round: Series A $4.5 million, announced July 16, 2017, led by Accel; any earlier post-YC seed financing is unknown. [Source](https://scale.com/blog/announcing-our-series-a-with-accel)
traction_at_yc: 40% weekly growth and over 50% gross margins. [Source](https://techcrunch.com/2016/08/22/y-combinator-demo-day-summer-2016/)
pivots: Expanded from a general human-task API into AI training-data infrastructure, then model evaluation and enterprise AI applications. [Original product](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/scale) [Later focus](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/scale-ai)
outcome: Still operating; Meta invested $14.3 billion in 2025, and Wang moved to Meta. Jason Droege succeeded him as CEO, with Meta holding a 49% stake. [Investment](https://apnews.com/article/4b55aabf7ea018e38ffdccb66e37cf26) [2026 status](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/06/scale-ai-jason-droege-reliable-ai)
key_lesson: Interpretation: making an overlooked manual bottleneck easy to access through software can create valuable infrastructure for a growing technology market.

name: FutureAdvisor
founding_story: Bo Lu and Jon Xu founded FutureAdvisor to make diversified, low-cost investment guidance available through software to people underserved by traditional financial advisers. The service initially analyzed existing investment accounts and recommended improvements. [Source](https://www.geekwire.com/2012/sequoia-capital-prominent-angels-invest-seattle-financial-advice-startup-futureadvisor/)
founders_background: Bo Lu: former Microsoft Windows Phone program manager. Co-founder Jon Xu, omitted from the input: former Microsoft engineer; education unknown. [Source](https://www.geekwire.com/2012/sequoia-capital-prominent-angels-invest-seattle-financial-advice-startup-futureadvisor/)

pre_funding_traces.note: No public trace verified before YC S10; the documented private beta preceded the March 2012 public launch, but was not established as predating YC.

how_they_got_funded: After YC S10, FutureAdvisor attracted Sequoia Capital and angels including Keith Rabois and Jeremy Stoppelman; a March 2012 report left the amount undisclosed. Sequoia invested another $5 million in August 2012. [Early investors](https://www.geekwire.com/2012/sequoia-capital-prominent-angels-invest-seattle-financial-advice-startup-futureadvisor/) [Later round](https://www.geekwire.com/2012/sequoia-sinks-5m-futureadvisor-transform-people-manage-investments/)
first_round_after_yc: unknown
pivots: Expanded from portfolio recommendations into managed robo-advice, then intermediary distribution under BlackRock; the retail business was transferred out in 2023. [Initial product](https://www.pcworld.com/article/469236/futureadvisor_launches_comprehensive_investment_advice_website.html) [Later changes](https://s3.amazonaws.com/fa-public/adv2.pdf)
outcome: BlackRock acquired FutureAdvisor in 2015. In 2023 its direct-to-retail business closed, with consenting clients transferred to Ritholtz Wealth Management. [Acquisition](https://s24.q4cdn.com/856567660/files/doc_financials/2015/ar/2015-Annual-Report.pdf) [Retail closure](https://www.investmentnews.com/fintech/blackrock-closes-futureadvisors-retail-business-moves-clients-to-ritholtz-wealth/234494)

failure_reasons.explanation: The retail closure and client transfer are documented, but the cited announcement does not establish a specific causal explanation.

key_lesson: Interpretation: acquisition can validate a financial technology product while leaving its original consumer service vulnerable to later strategic changes.

name: Rigetti Computing
founding_story: Chad Rigetti founded the company in 2013 to build commercially useful quantum computers, ultimately combining quantum processors with conventional computing. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/rigetti-computing) [Company timeline](https://www.rigetti.com/uploads/Rigetti-Investor-Presentation.pdf)
founders_background: Chad Rigetti: physicist with a Yale PhD and prior work in IBM's quantum-computing group from 2010 to 2013. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/rigetti-computing) [Company biography](https://www.rigetti.com/uploads/January-2022-Investor-Presentation.pdf)

pre_funding_traces.note: Rigetti co-authored a superconducting-qubit coherence paper published in September 2012 while affiliated with IBM, before company formation and YC S14; this was prior founder research, not a company product.

how_they_got_funded: Rigetti joined YC S14 and raised a reported $2.5 million seed round in 2014 from investors including AME Cloud Ventures, Morado, Susa, Felicis and YC. It later accessed public capital through a SPAC combination. [Seed](https://nqit.ox.ac.uk/sites/www.nqit.ox.ac.uk/files/2018-10/Commercial%20Prospects%20for%20Quantum%20Computing%20Dec%202016.pdf) [Public financing](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2022/03/02/2395179/0/en/rigetti-computing-announces-closing-of-business-combination-with-supernova-partners-acquisition-company-ii-ltd-begins-trading-on-nasdaq-capital-market-today.html)
first_round_after_yc: unknown; a $2.5 million seed round was reported in August 2014, during the YC S14 period, so its status as strictly post-YC is unverified. [Date](https://srfc.law/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/DealFlow-820.pdf) [Investors](https://nqit.ox.ac.uk/sites/www.nqit.ox.ac.uk/files/2018-10/Commercial%20Prospects%20for%20Quantum%20Computing%20Dec%202016.pdf)
pivots: none verified; the company developed its hybrid quantum/classical architecture and dedicated fabrication capability over time. [Source](https://www.rigetti.com/uploads/Rigetti-Investor-Presentation.pdf)
outcome: Became publicly traded on Nasdaq as RGTI on March 2, 2022, after its Supernova Partners II combination, receiving approximately $261.75 million in gross proceeds. [Source](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2022/03/02/2395179/0/en/rigetti-computing-announces-closing-of-business-combination-with-supernova-partners-acquisition-company-ii-ltd-begins-trading-on-nasdaq-capital-market-today.html)
key_lesson: Interpretation: founder research can establish technical credibility well before commercial traction, but hardware development requires multiple financing stages.

name: Brex
founding_story: Henrique Dubugras and Pedro Franceschi entered YC W17 with a virtual-reality idea, then pivoted three weeks into the program to corporate cards for venture-backed startups lacking conventional credit histories. [Source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brex)
founders_background: Both founders previously built and sold Brazilian payments company Pagar.me, moved to the United States to attend Stanford in 2016, and dropped out within a year to start Brex. [Source](https://time.com/6292852/brex-ceo-henrique-dubugras-silicon-valley-bank/)

pre_funding_traces.note: The founders' earlier payments venture Pagar.me had been built and sold before Brex and YC; this is prior founder operating evidence, not proof that Brex itself had customers before funding.

how_they_got_funded: After YC W17, Brex raised a $7 million Series A in spring 2017 led by Ribbit Capital, with investors including YC, Peter Thiel and Max Levchin. A $50 million Series B followed in 2018. [Initial round](https://app.dealroom.co/companies/brex) [Subsequent financing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brex)
first_round_after_yc: Series A $7 million, spring 2017, led by Ribbit Capital; sources differ on March versus April timing. [Round database](https://app.dealroom.co/companies/brex) [Founder interview](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/y-combinator-startup-podcast/82-henrique-dubugras-of-brex-and-anu-hariharan)
pivots: Virtual reality to startup corporate cards during YC; subsequently expanded into business accounts and spend-management software. [Early pivot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brex) [Expanded product](https://www.capitalone.com/about/newsroom/capital-one-completes-acquisition-of-brex/)
outcome: Capital One completed the acquisition on April 7, 2026. The announced deal value was $5.15 billion; subsequent filings recorded approximately $4.5 billion in consideration paid, with Pedro Franceschi continuing as CEO. [Completion](https://www.capitalone.com/about/newsroom/capital-one-completes-acquisition-of-brex/) [Announced value](https://www.brex.com/journal/brex-and-capital-one-join-forces) [Closing consideration](https://investor.capitalone.com/static-files/8e50afd5-c02c-474c-99bb-e7753d8a8f9d)
key_lesson: Interpretation: returning to an area of prior expertise can reveal an underserved customer segment and support a rapid early pivot.

name: HelloSign
founding_story: Joseph Walla started HelloFax to solve his own difficulty sending faxes; feedback on Hacker News encouraged him to build a company. He and Neal O'Mara subsequently recognized demand for its signing feature and launched HelloSign in August 2012. [Origin](https://betakit.com/hellofax-launches-hellosign-to-take-on-electronic-signature-industry/), [launch](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/hellofax-yc-w11-launches-hellosign-the-easies/)
founders_background: Neal O'Mara: technical cofounder and CTO; earlier employment and education unknown. Joseph Walla, omitted from the input founder list, was cofounder and CEO; earlier background unknown. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/hellosign), [Dropbox](https://investors.dropbox.com/node/7141/pdf)

pre_funding_traces.note: An early Hacker News idea post generated feedback before Walla decided to turn HelloFax into a company; the retrospective does not establish the exact posting or first-investment date.

how_they_got_funded: HelloFax participated in YC Winter 2011. Walla reported $3.5 million raised cumulatively by December 2016; a $16 million Series B led by Foundry Group and Zach Coelius followed in June 2017. The exact earliest post-YC round is unknown. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/hellosign), [founder interview](https://broadcasts.com/podcasts/saas-interviews-with-ceos-startups-founders/ep-517-35m-raised-6m-users-helping-47k-customers-s/), [Series B](https://www.prweb.com/releases/hellosign_announces_16_million_series_b_investment_to_fuel_enterprise_growth/prweb14415002.htm)
first_round_after_yc: unknown
pivots: Expanded from online faxing into standalone electronic signatures in 2012 after recognizing that signing was a market of its own. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/hellofax-yc-w11-launches-hellosign-the-easies/)
outcome: Acquired by Dropbox in 2019 for $230 million in cash. [Acquisition announcement](https://investors.dropbox.com/node/7141/pdf), [YC acquired status](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/hellosign)
key_lesson: Inference: close attention to how customers use one feature can reveal a larger standalone business.

name: GitPrime
founding_story: Travis Kimmel and Ben Thompson started GitPrime while working at DurangoSpace, seeking better ways to evaluate software engineering progress. Kimmel's engineering management experience and Thompson's product design work exposed the same measurement problem. [Local reporting](https://www.durangoherald.com/articles/news/startup-software-company-gitprime-aims-to-be-major-employer/)
founders_background: Travis Kimmel: previously managed software engineers. Ben Thompson: worked in digital product design. Education unknown for both. [Backgrounds](https://www.durangoherald.com/articles/news/startup-software-company-gitprime-aims-to-be-major-employer/)

pre_funding_traces.note: No public trace was verified as preceding the first outside investment. Reporting places initial product development and seed funding in 2015, before YC; their precise ordering is unknown.

how_they_got_funded: Obtained seed funding in 2015 before joining YC Winter 2016; also participated in Durango's SCAPE accelerator. In April 2018 it announced a $10.5 million Series A led by OpenView with existing investor Data Collective, bringing reported total funding to $13 million. [Early history](https://www.durangoherald.com/articles/news/startup-software-company-gitprime-aims-to-be-major-employer/), [Series A](https://www.privateequityinternational.com/gitprime-raises-10-5-mln/)
first_round_after_yc: A $200,000 offering had its first sale in April 2016, according to an SEC-filing index; investors and round label unknown. [Filing index](https://fundraisingfox.com/companies/gitprime)
traction_at_yc: Demo Day reporting named SolarCity, Ooyala and Sphero as customers and reported 73% month-over-month growth; the growth metric was unspecified. [Demo Day](https://techcrunch.com/2016/03/23/y-combinator-winter-2016/)
pivots: none
outcome: Pluralsight acquired GitPrime for approximately $170 million in May 2019. Its successor product, Flow, transferred to Appfire in February 2025 and is scheduled for retirement on December 31, 2027. [Acquisition](https://www.pluralsight.com/newsroom/press-releases/pluralsight-to-acquire-gitprime), [Appfire notice](https://appfire.com/flow/info)
key_lesson: Inference: firsthand management problems can support a valuable specialist product, although an acquisition does not guarantee its indefinite continuation.

name: Clever
founding_story: Clever began in 2012 when Dan Carroll's school technology work revealed how much time schools lost managing logins and moving student data. He teamed up with Harvard classmates Rafael Garcia and Tyler Bosmeny to simplify those integrations. [Founder account](https://www.clever.com/blog/2017/05/clevers-5th-birthday-celebrate), [Harvard profile](https://seas.harvard.edu/news/alumni-profile-rafael-garcia-ab-09)
founders_background: Dan Carroll: Harvard human evolutionary biology and computer science studies; data and technology director for a Denver school district. Rafael Garcia: Harvard applied math and computer science studies; worked in finance. Tyler Bosmeny, omitted from the input: Harvard applied math and master's in statistics; worked at a San Francisco startup. [Harvard](https://seas.harvard.edu/news/alumni-profile-rafael-garcia-ab-09)

pre_funding_traces.note: No public product, customer or launch trace was verified as predating YC funding; the documented June 2012 launch and subsequent school adoption occurred during the YC period.

how_they_got_funded: Joined YC Summer 2012 and greatly exceeded Paul Graham's target of integrating 40 schools. In October 2012 it announced $3 million in seed funding from investors including SV Angel, Floodgate, SoftTech VC, Google Ventures and Bessemer. Sequoia partnered with the company in 2013. [Seed and YC growth](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/clever-yc-s12-raises-3m-has-now-unlocked-k12), [Sequoia](https://sequoiacap.com/companies/clever)
first_round_after_yc: Seed $3 million, announced October 22, 2012; investors included SV Angel, Floodgate, SoftTech VC, Google Ventures and Bessemer; lead unknown. [YC announcement](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/clever-yc-s12-raises-3m-has-now-unlocked-k12)
traction_at_yc: Reached 1,000 schools by August 2012 Demo Day, against a target of 40; exceeded 2,000 schools by October. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/clever-yc-s12-raises-3m-has-now-unlocked-k12)
pivots: Expanded from student-data integrations into single sign-on and account provisioning. [Harvard profile](https://seas.harvard.edu/news/alumni-profile-rafael-garcia-ab-09)
outcome: Kahoot completed its acquisition in September 2021 at an enterprise value of $435–500 million, including up to $65 million contingent on performance; Clever continued under its own brand. [Completion announcement](https://kahoot.com/press/2021/09/02/kahoot-completes-acquisition-clever/)
key_lesson: Inference: removing an operational bottleneck can create infrastructure that benefits both users and their software suppliers.

name: Sendwave
founding_story: Drew Durbin and Lincoln Quirk entered YC in 2012 with Chime, a social app, then tried several social products before starting Sendwave in early 2014. Durbin's experience in Africa and positive interviews with Kenyan immigrants encouraged them to tackle remittances despite the regulatory complexity. [Cofounder account](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/2023/10/23/entrepreneurship_advice.html)
founders_background: Drew Durbin: attended Brown University and had worked in Africa. Lincoln Quirk, omitted from the input: Brown computer science graduate, Harvard PhD dropout and programmer who had previously attempted a programming-language startup. [Durbin](https://www.crunchbase.com/person/drew-durbin), [Quirk resume](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/resume.html), [founder account](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/2023/10/23/entrepreneurship_advice.html)

pre_funding_traces.note: No dated public trace before the original company's YC investment was verified. Chime preceded Sendwave, but the remittance interviews and prototype were undertaken after YC and therefore do not qualify as pre-funding evidence.

how_they_got_funded: The founders obtained YC Winter 2012 backing for Chime and later pivoted to remittances. A May 2016 SEC notice for Chime Inc., naming Durbin and Quirk, disclosed $9,525,771 sold in an equity offering whose first sale was May 13, 2016; investors were not named, and whether this was the first post-YC round is unknown. [Founder history](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/2023/10/23/entrepreneurship_advice.html), [SEC filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1625286/000162528616000001/xslFormDX01/primary_doc.xml)
first_round_after_yc: unknown
pivots: Chime's event discovery, chat, dating and video-chat experiments gave way to Sendwave's remittance service in 2014; Sendwave itself did not exist during the 2012 YC batch. [Cofounder account](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/2023/10/23/entrepreneurship_advice.html)
outcome: WorldRemit announced the acquisition in 2020 and completed it in 2021; Quirk's resume reports a $500 million sale. Sendwave continued as a brand within the group. [Completion](https://www.worldremit.com/en/news/worldremit-completes-sendwave-acquisition-and-appoints-two-executives), [founder resume](https://www.lincolnquirk.com/resume.html)
key_lesson: Inference: direct customer research can justify tackling a difficult, regulated problem after easier-looking ideas fail to gain traction.

name: Presto
founding_story: Rajat Suri founded E la Carte, later Presto, in 2008 after experiencing the difficulty of splitting a restaurant bill with friends. He developed restaurant ordering and payment tablets and worked as a waiter to understand restaurant operations. [Origin](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/e-la-carte-yc-w10-on-the-right-way-to-go-after-big-clients/), [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presto_%28restaurant_technology_platform%29)
founders_background: Rajat Suri: former MIT graduate student who left his program; previously co-founded Zimride and gained firsthand restaurant experience as a waiter. [History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presto_%28restaurant_technology_platform%29)

pre_funding_traces.note: Romulus seeded E la Carte in 2008, before YC. No public trace was verified as preceding that investment; early restaurant pilots cannot confidently be classified as pre-funding.

how_they_got_funded: Romulus provided seed funding in 2008, followed by YC in 2010. Lightbank invested $4 million in August 2011, and Intel Capital led a $13.5 million Series B in 2013 with Romulus participating. [Early investor](https://news.mit.edu/2016/alum-venture-capital-tech-startups-0714), [funding history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presto_%28restaurant_technology_platform%29)
first_round_after_yc: First clearly identified named round found: $4 million from Lightbank, August 2011; whether an intervening seed financing occurred is unknown. [History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presto_%28restaurant_technology_platform%29)
pivots: Shifted from tabletop ordering and payment devices toward drive-through voice AI; exited the Presto Touch business when its final customer contracts expired in June 2024. [SEC filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1822145/000101376224001164/ea020687602-424b5_presto.htm)
outcome: Went public through a SPAC in September 2022, but was delisted in September 2024. Following a loan default, assets were sold through an Article 9 process to a Remus Capital-led consortium; the January 2025 announcement described continued operations under Presto Phoenix. [Public listing](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/presto), [delisting](https://www.sec.gov/enforcement-litigation/administrative-proceedings/33-11352-s), [asset sale](https://investor.presto.com/news-releases/news-release-details/presto-automation-announces-sale-assets-consortium-led-remus)

failure_reasons.explanation: Persistent financing problems culminated in default on the Metropolitan Partners loan, allowing foreclosure on the company's assets.
The company was unable to find a buyer for its debt or complete refinancing before the lender takeover process.

key_lesson: Inference: a public listing and promising new product do not remove the need to fund a business transition before debt obligations become unmanageable.

name: Razorpay
founding_story: Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar encountered payment-gateway obstacles while building an online donation project in 2014. They shifted to making online payments accessible to Indian startups and small businesses. [Founder account](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/razorpay)
founders_background: Both met at IIT Roorkee, enjoyed coding and helped establish SDS Labs. Mathur worked at Schlumberger after graduation; Kumar moved to the United States to work at Microsoft. [Founder account](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/razorpay)

pre_funding_traces.note: The founders describe college coding projects and a donation-platform precursor, but no dated public Razorpay launch, customer or repository trace was verified as preceding outside funding.

how_they_got_funded: Accepted into YC in late 2014 for Winter 2015 and launched at its March Demo Day. The founders announced a seed round backed by Matrix Partners, YC and 33 angels, followed by a $9 million Series A led by Tiger Global with Matrix; the company reported $11.5 million across both rounds. [Founder history](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/razorpay), [company announcement](https://razorpay.com/blog/series-a-funding-2/), [round amounts](https://www.business-standard.com/article/companies/fintech-start-up-razorpay-secures-9-million-in-series-a-funding-115102700512_1.html)
first_round_after_yc: Seed approximately $2.5 million, 2015, backed by Matrix Partners, YC and 33 angels; some databases report $2.6 million. [Contemporaneous reporting](https://www.business-standard.com/article/companies/fintech-start-up-razorpay-secures-9-million-in-series-a-funding-115102700512_1.html), [database](https://app.dealroom.co/companies/razorpay)
traction_at_yc: Mathur retrospectively reported 300 businesses signing up on launch day; the company dates its launch to March 2015 Demo Day. [Founder interview](https://yourstory.com/2019/07/mavericks-harshil-mathur-startup-razorpay), [launch date](https://razorpay.com/blog/series-a-funding-2/)
pivots: Moved from a donation-platform project to payment infrastructure, then expanded from a payment gateway into a broader financial product suite. [YC profile](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/razorpay)
outcome: Still operating; YC lists it as active, offering payments and banking products for businesses. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/razorpay)
key_lesson: Inference: infrastructure difficulties encountered while building one product can expose a larger opportunity serving other businesses.

name: EquipmentShare
founding_story: Construction veterans Jabbok and William Schlacks developed EquipmentShare to address idle equipment, downtime and poor visibility across jobsites. Their idea won Startup Weekend Columbia in 2014 before the company joined YC Winter 2015. [Company history](https://www.equipmentshare.com/press-releases/startupweekend-columbia-is-back-this-time-at-an-alumnis-hq), [problem](https://www.equipmentshare.com/media-kit)
founders_background: Jabbok and William 'Willy' Schlacks: lifelong contractors raised in rural Missouri, with extensive practical construction experience. Brad Siegler and Jeff Lowe: YC-listed cofounders and members of the winning Startup Weekend team; earlier jobs and education unknown. [YC history](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/congratulations-to-equipmentshare), [founder roster](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/equipmentshare), [competition team](https://www.equipmentshare.com/press-releases/startupweekend-columbia-is-back-this-time-at-an-alumnis-hq)

pre_funding_traces.note: Won Startup Weekend Columbia in 2014, before YC Winter 2015; this is a dated public precursor to its recorded institutional funding.

how_they_got_funded: Joined YC Winter 2015 and connected with Romulus during the program. Raised a reported $2.1 million seed round in May 2015 with investors including Romulus, YC, Great Oaks and FundersClub; a $5.5 million Series A followed in May 2016. Romulus described a fit with its investment theme around enterprise asset sharing. [Investor account](https://romuluscap.squarespace.com/equipment-share), [funding record](https://app.dealroom.co/companies/equipmentshare_com), [company timeline](https://www.equipmentshare.com/about)
first_round_after_yc: Seed $2.1 million, May 2015; investors included Romulus Capital, YC, Great Oaks Venture Capital and FundersClub. [Funding record](https://app.dealroom.co/companies/equipmentshare_com)
pivots: Evolved from contractor-to-contractor equipment sharing into a nationwide rental operation integrated with proprietary fleet and jobsite technology. [Early model](https://romuluscap.squarespace.com/equipment-share), [current business](https://www.equipmentshare.com/media-kit)
outcome: Went public in January 2026 and continues operating its equipment rental and construction technology business. [YC IPO announcement](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/congratulations-to-equipmentshare), [company](https://www.equipmentshare.com/media-kit)
key_lesson: Inference: deep industry experience can reveal an opportunity to combine software with the physical operations needed to deliver customer value.

name: Fivestars
founding_story: Victor Ho and Matt Doka started Fivestars to bring customer loyalty tools to local merchants. Ho had previously worked on loyalty strategies for large companies, and the founders acquired early merchants by selling door to door. [YC biography](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fivestars), [early sales account](https://tollbit.forbes.com/sites/brucerogers/2014/07/30/bringing-customer-loyalty-programs-to-local-merchants/2/)
founders_background: Victor Ho: Goldman Sachs investment banker, then McKinsey consultant working on loyalty and customer engagement; Berkeley degrees in industrial engineering, rhetoric and business administration. Matt Doka: cofounder and CTO; previously worked at Goldman Sachs and McKinsey according to the founders' profile; education unknown. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fivestars), [profile](https://tollbit.forbes.com/sites/brucerogers/2014/07/30/bringing-customer-loyalty-programs-to-local-merchants/2/)

pre_funding_traces.note: Door-to-door sales and initial merchant adoption are documented in early 2011, but were not verified as preceding the January 2011 YC investment.

how_they_got_funded: Participated in YC Winter 2011, followed by a reported $2 million seed financing in April 2011 involving Mayfield, DCM and angels. In August 2012 YC reported a $13.9 million round involving Lightspeed and DCM, alongside YC, Mayfield and angels. [Seed history](https://app.dealroom.co/companies/fivestars), [2012 announcement](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/fivestars-yc-w11-raises-139m-from-lightspeed/)
first_round_after_yc: Seed $2 million, April 2011; investors included Mayfield, DCM, Chamath Palihapitiya and Eric Stein. [Funding record](https://app.dealroom.co/companies/fivestars)
pivots: Expanded from customer loyalty programs into an integrated marketing and payments platform. [Acquisition description](https://fsweb.fivestars.com/about-us/sumup-to-acquire-fivestars/)
outcome: SumUp completed its acquisition on October 28, 2021 for $317 million in cash and stock. [Completion announcement](https://www.sumup.com/en-us/press/fivestarsacquisition/)
key_lesson: Inference: adapting enterprise practices for small businesses requires a practical product and a repeatable way to reach merchants.

name: Coinbase
founding_story: Brian Armstrong started Coinbase to make Bitcoin usable without intimidating desktop software and complicated purchasing steps. He applied to YC in March 2012 with an unlaunched project called Bitbank; Fred Ehrsam subsequently joined as a cofounder. [YC history](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/coinbase-from-yc-to-ipo/)
founders_background: Brian Armstrong: former Airbnb software engineer who helped build fraud prevention systems. Fred Ehrsam, omitted from the input: former Goldman Sachs trader. [YC history](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/coinbase-from-yc-to-ipo/), [funding announcement](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/coinbase-yc-s12-raises-5m-from-union-square-ventures-largest-financing-round-yet-for-a-bitcoin-startup)

pre_funding_traces.note: Armstrong's March 2012 YC application described an earlier Android Bitcoin app built as a side project; distribution, usage and traction figures are unknown. Coinbase itself had not launched at application time.

how_they_got_funded: Joined YC Summer 2012, then raised a $600,000 seed round in September 2012. Initialized invested at Demo Day despite broad investor skepticism; Union Square Ventures led a $5 million Series A in May 2013. [Early investor history](https://www.newcomer.co/p/the-golden-ticket), [round announcement](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/coinbase-yc-s12-raises-5m-from-union-square-ventures-largest-financing-round-yet-for-a-bitcoin-startup)
first_round_after_yc: Seed $600,000, September 2012; investors included Initialized and other early backers; lead unknown. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/coinbase-yc-s12-raises-5m-from-union-square-ventures-largest-financing-round-yet-for-a-bitcoin-startup), [investor history](https://www.newcomer.co/p/the-golden-ticket)
traction_at_yc: Signups grew 20% daily between August 10 and August 17, 2012. [YC retrospective](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/coinbase-from-yc-to-ipo/)
pivots: Expanded from a hosted Bitcoin wallet into a platform for buying, selling and managing multiple cryptocurrencies. [Early product](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/coinbase-from-yc-to-ipo/), [company profile](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/coinbase)
outcome: Became publicly traded on April 14, 2021 and remains listed as public in YC's directory. [Listing retrospective](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/coinbase-from-yc-to-ipo/), [YC profile](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/coinbase)
key_lesson: Inference: making a difficult emerging technology approachable can create strong demand before most investors accept the underlying market.

name: Bird
founding_story: MessageBird, now Bird, grew out of unreliable verification SMS at Robert Vis's previous company, Zaypay. The team built its own carrier connection, launched a messaging product in 2010, and established MessageBird in 2011 after demand emerged from its former messaging supplier. [Founder account](https://medium.com/messagebird/messagebird-raises-60m-series-a-funding-9c703f95c67e)
founders_background: Robert Vis: previously ran mobile payments company Zaypay. Bob Violier: technical founding-team member and YC-listed CTO; earlier career and education unknown. Joey van Ommen: YC-listed product founder; his own departure post says he joined when the company had approximately 15 people, so his status as an original founder is unclear; earlier background unknown. [Founder account](https://medium.com/messagebird/messagebird-raises-60m-series-a-funding-9c703f95c67e), [YC roster](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/bird), [Joey's account](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/joeyvanommen_after-8-years-at-messagebird-ive-decided-activity-7141000109521108992-u4II)

pre_funding_traces.note: The messaging infrastructure originated inside Zaypay in 2010 before MessageBird's formation and YC participation; whether Zaypay itself had outside funding is unknown.
Bootstrapped MessageBird generated $20 million revenue and positive $2 million EBITA in 2015, before YC Summer 2016.

how_they_got_funded: Bootstrapped before participating in YC Summer 2016. In October 2017 it raised a $60 million Series A led by Accel with significant participation from Atomico and participation from YC; Vis said the capital would expand its team, global awareness and balance sheet. [Funding announcement](https://medium.com/messagebird/messagebird-raises-60m-series-a-funding-9c703f95c67e), [funding context](https://www.investing.com/news/technology-news/messagebird-in-biggest-earlystage-funding-for-european-software-firm-536086)
first_round_after_yc: Series A $60 million, October 2017, led by Accel with Atomico and YC participating. [Founder announcement](https://medium.com/messagebird/messagebird-raises-60m-series-a-funding-9c703f95c67e)
traction_at_yc: Entered YC as a five-year-old profitable business; 2015 revenue was $20 million with $2 million positive EBITA. [Contemporaneous reporting](https://techcrunch.com/2016/07/08/a-rare-bird-indeed/)
pivots: Expanded from SMS infrastructure across communications channels, rebranded as Bird in 2024, and now describes its direction as communications infrastructure for AI agents. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/bird), [company history](https://bird.com/about)
outcome: Still operating as Bird; YC lists it as active, and its current website markets communications infrastructure for developers and AI agents. [YC](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/bird), [company](https://bird.com/about)
key_lesson: Inference: a profitable business built around an internal need can use venture funding later to accelerate an already established market opportunity.

name: CleverDeck
founding_story: Justin Cannon created CleverDeck as a vocabulary-learning app using spaced repetition, images and native-speaker audio; the specific founding motivation is unknown. Its YC listing mixes this description with the art-commissioning business EveryArt, which contemporaneous coverage identifies as Cannon's W12 company. Sources: https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/cleverdeck ; https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/with-everyart-yc-w12-you-dont-have-to-be-afra
founders_background: Justin Cannon previously founded language-learning company Lingt; his public product profile also identifies him as founder of Turkish Tea Time. Education: unknown. Source: https://pitchwall.co/product/cleverdeck

pre_funding_traces.note: A November 2011 public letter lists Cannon with Lingt Language and EveryArt, establishing a public predecessor-company trace before W12; no pre-funding CleverDeck product trace was verified.

how_they_got_funded: Cannon's EveryArt participated in YC W12. Databases attribute YC funding to the current CleverDeck listing, but the relationship between the two businesses and any separate financing of CleverDeck are unknown. Sources: https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/with-everyart-yc-w12-you-dont-have-to-be-afra ; https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/cleverdeck
first_round_after_yc: unknown
pivots: The YC record changed from EveryArt's art-commissioning marketplace to CleverDeck's language flashcards; whether this was a corporate pivot or a reused founder/company listing is unknown. Sources: https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/cleverdeck ; https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/with-everyart-yc-w12-you-dont-have-to-be-afra
outcome: YC labels CleverDeck Active, but independent confirmation of current operations is unknown. EveryArt was reported as apparently shut down by January 2014. Sources: https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/cleverdeck ; https://techcrunch.com/2014/01/14/artcorgi-launch/
key_lesson: Research inference: reconcile historical product names before attributing an accelerator history or funding round to a later product.

name: Wifi Dabba, Inc.
founding_story: While onboarding taxi drivers to their Stepni app in 2016, Karam Lakshman and Shubhendu Sharma found that expensive, unreliable connectivity prevented regular use. They began supplying inexpensive public Wi-Fi through neighborhood shops. Source: https://yourstory.com/2020/01/wifi-dabba-startup-provides-free-wifi-bengaluru
founders_background: Karam Lakshman previously ran the internet and mobile fund at CIIE, IIM Ahmedabad. Shubhendu Sharma worked at Mahindra British Telecom and has a telecom-product background; contemporary reporting describes him as an engineer with an IIM Bangalore MBA. Sources: https://in.dabba.com/ ; https://yourstory.com/2017/11/wifi-cheaper-than-cutting-chai-wifi-dabba

pre_funding_traces.note: In 2016, the founders built a Raspberry Pi router and tested it at a tea stall near their office; dozens of people connected within hours. This predates W17, although an earlier outside-investment date could not be established.

how_they_got_funded: Joined YC W17 and subsequently described its financing as seed money from YC and other investors. The application story, additional investors' entry dates and a reliable post-YC round amount are unknown. Sources: https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/wifi-dabba-inc ; https://yourstory.com/2017/11/wifi-cheaper-than-cutting-chai-wifi-dabba
first_round_after_yc: unknown
traction_at_yc: By March 2017 it was selling small internet packages through tea stalls and bakeries, including 100MB for approximately $0.03; user count and revenue are unknown. Source: https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/yc-w17-launch-lively-scaphold-marketfox-floyd-servx-fibo-and-wifi-dabba/
pivots: Expanded from prepaid public hotspots into co-living connectivity and laser-based middle-mile infrastructure, later adopting community-owned, blockchain-based hotspot financing. Sources: https://yourstory.com/2020/01/wifi-dabba-startup-provides-free-wifi-bengaluru ; https://in.dabba.com/
outcome: Operating as Dabba, offering hotspot ownership and deployment through local cable operators in India. Source: https://in.dabba.com/
key_lesson: Research inference: a distribution problem encountered in one startup can reveal a more fundamental infrastructure business.

name: Reclaim Protocol
founding_story: Reclaim emerged from identity-verification needs within Questbook and developed into a standalone protocol for proving information from websites. CreatorOS identifies Questbook as its original public product and Reclaim as its current flagship. Sources: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JApgPz9uuAs ; https://www.socionity.com/
founders_background: Madhavan Malolan leads product, engineering and research; previously worked at Microsoft and Samosa Labs and studied at IIIT Hyderabad. Sriharsha Karamchati earned a research master's in computer security and algorithms at IIIT Hyderabad and previously built Questbook. Sources: https://www.ycombinator.com/founders/madhavan-malolan ; https://crypto.stanford.edu/seclab/sem-24-25/karamchati.html

pre_funding_traces.note: No public product trace was verified as preceding the October 2020 pre-seed financing recorded for CreatorOS/Questbook; later tutorials, grants tools and Reclaim repositories do not establish pre-funding activity.

how_they_got_funded: Funding databases record a $625,000 pre-seed in October 2020 and a March 2021 seed associated with the W21 period. CreatorOS confirms that Questbook raised an $8.3 million Series A in 2022 led by Lemniscap, with Coinbase Ventures, Dragonfly, Hashed and Polygon participating. Sources: https://aventure.vc/companies/reclaim-protocol-questbook-hyderabad-in/fundraising ; https://www.socionity.com/
first_round_after_yc: First clearly verified later round: Series A $8.3M, 2022, led by Lemniscap; the March 2021 seed's timing relative to YC completion is unknown. Sources: https://www.socionity.com/ ; https://aventure.vc/companies/reclaim-protocol-questbook-hyderabad-in/fundraising
pivots: Questbook developed developer education and grant-allocation products; Reclaim subsequently became the company's flagship verification infrastructure. Sources: https://inc42.com/buzz/web3-startup-questbook-raises-8-3-mn-help-web3-developers-access-capital/ ; https://www.socionity.com/
outcome: Operating, with CreatorOS focused on Reclaim's cryptographic verification of credentials and other user claims. Source: https://www.socionity.com/
key_lesson: Research inference: infrastructure built to solve an internal verification problem can become the company's main product.

name: InfluxData
founding_story: Paul Dix and Todd Persen started Errplane in 2012 to provide real-time monitoring. When customer adoption disappointed, they turned the time-series infrastructure they needed internally into InfluxDB. Source: https://www.influxdata.com/blog/influxdb-1-0-ga-released-a-retrospective-and-whats-next/
founders_background: Paul Dix is a software engineer with a Columbia computer-science degree, experience at Google, Microsoft and McAfee, and a published book on Ruby/Rails service design. Todd Persen, omitted from the input founder list, is identified by Dix as his original cofounder; further background unknown. name: Bitmovin
founding_story: Bitmovin grew out of MPEG-DASH streaming research at the University of Klagenfurt, commercializing technology for delivering online video. Its company history dates the research beginnings to 2012 and first products to 2014. Source: https://bitmovin.com/about-us/
founders_background: Stefan Lederer and Christopher Mueller conducted streaming research at the University of Klagenfurt; Christian Timmerer collaborated with them there. All three coauthored a 2012 DASH dataset paper. Sources: https://bitmovin.com/about-us/ ; https://dash.itec.aau.at/dash-dataset/

pre_funding_traces.note: Lederer, Mueller and Timmerer published Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP Dataset at ACM MMSys in February 2012, preceding the reported August 2014 commercial seed financing; this was university research, not evidence that the underlying research was unfunded.

how_they_got_funded: Raised a seven-figure seed financing in August 2014, before joining YC S15 and opening a US office. Later funding included a 2016 Series A and subsequent growth rounds. Sources: https://www.streamingmediaglobal.com/Articles/News/Featured-News/Bitmovin-Raises-7-Figure-Seed-Funding-Plans-International-Growth-98687.aspx ; https://bitmovin.com/about-us/
first_round_after_yc: An August 2015 seed round is recorded at $850K; lead investor unknown. A larger Series A followed in 2016. Sources: https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/66003-22 ; https://bitmovin.com/about-us/
pivots: Shifted toward a developer-focused go-to-market strategy during 2015; no unrelated product pivot verified. Source: https://bitmovin.com/about-us/
outcome: Operating as a privately owned video-infrastructure company; reports a $25M Series C in 2021. Source: https://bitmovin.com/about-us/
key_lesson: Research inference: academic standards work can create commercial advantages, but international sales still require a deliberate distribution strategy.

name: Dashworks

Praty Sharma previously worked as a machine-learning engineer at Facebook; further verified education and employment details are unknown. first_round_after_yc: unknown; a $4M round led by Point72 was announced in January 2022, but earlier rounds are recorded without a consistently verified chronology. name: DeepSource
founding_story: Sanket Saurav and Jai Pradeesh began DeepSource in 2018 to automate objective code-review work and make static analysis easier to adopt. The initial Python/GitHub product launched in March 2019. Sources: https://www.gaebler.com/Funded-Company-21E71291-F2AF-45F3-AB4B-5831D665E062-DeepSource ; https://yourstory.com/companies/deepsource
founders_background: Sanket Saurav is a software entrepreneur who had worked on earlier startups. key_lesson: Research inference: developer-tool adoption depends on fitting existing workflows and producing findings users trust.

name: Landed

founders_background: Jonathan Asmis began as a biomedical engineer making vaccines, later worked on social-impact bonds and energy-storage finance, and earned a Stanford MBA. Alex Lofton worked on Obama's 2007–08 field campaign, held social-enterprise and startup roles, worked at Forest City, and holds Northwestern and Stanford degrees. Jesse Vaughan is an additional cofounder; background unknown. Sources: https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/landed ; https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/alumni/news/catalyst/jonathan-asmis-mba-15 ; https://landed.com/mission-and-history

pre_funding_traces.note: No public launch, customer or prototype trace was verified as preceding first outside funding; a 2015 founding date alone does not establish such a trace.

name: Elemeno Health

pre_funding_traces.note: No company-specific public launch or traction trace could be confidently dated before its first outside investment; Signature Ventures identifies a 2020 pre-seed investment without an exact date.
